cultivar: Qing Xin Oolong and Jin Xuan, the main Ren'ai cultivars
processing: Little is recorded for this village alone. Ren'ai teas are typically lightly oxidised and semi-ball rolled.
harvest_season: Not specifically documented; spring is usual for Ren'ai high-mountain oolong.
appearance_dry: Typically tight, deep-green semi-rolled balls, as with other Ren'ai oolongs.
appearance_liquor: Typically pale clear yellow-green, as with other Ren'ai oolongs.
appearance_wet: Typically thick green leaves that open fully, as with other Ren'ai oolongs.
taste_profile: No tasting record exists for Aowanda alone. Ren'ai high-mountain teas are typically floral and sweet with low bitterness.

brewing.notes: General high-mountain oolong brewing: hot water, a long first steep and shorter ones afterwards.

vintage_note: Usual for its class rather than documented for this place: sold by harvest of the current year and drunk fresh, usually within a year or so. Ren'ai gardens are scattered and much is sold under the general label of high-mountain tea, so an Aowanda name on a packet is uncommon.
description:
Aowanda is an area in Ren'ai Township, Nantou, better known to most Taiwanese for its forest recreation area than for tea. It is listed among the township's tea-growing places, and tea from there would fall within the wider Ren'ai high-mountain category.

Ren'ai grows mainly Qing Xin Oolong and Jin Xuan, and its tea usually follows the light-oxidation, rolled-ball model. How this particular spot differs from its neighbours is not recorded.

So treat it as a Ren'ai oolong: floral, sweet, with low bitterness, brewed hot. If you find one, ask the seller which garden and which harvest, since the name alone tells you little.
history: Little is documented about tea at Aowanda specifically. It appears among the tea-producing localities of Ren'ai, a district where commercial growing was first promoted around Wushe and Gaofeng and whose teas are often sold under the general high-mountain label because the gardens are so dispersed.
